## Context

- **Audience:** early-career PhD researchers who have used linear models but have not met mixed models before.
- **Place in the curriculum:** first session of [Module B3, Mixed models](curriculum.qmd#track-b). It builds on B1 (linear models) and B2 (GLMs).
- **Length:** a 15-minute version for the demonstration; in the course, the same input is followed by about an hour of hands-on work.

## Learning goals

By the end of the session, students will be able to:

1. **Recognise** when their data are grouped (repeated trials, siblings, individuals in social groups) and why that breaks the independence assumption.
2. **Explain** what a random intercept is and what the intraclass correlation tells them.
3. **Choose** between a linear mixed model and a GLMM based on the type of their response.
4. **Interpret** the coefficients of a GLMM as effects for the *typical individual*.

## Structure

| Part | What happens | Goal |
|:--|:--|:--:|
| One model, many names | t-test, regression, ANOVA, ANCOVA and GLMs as one family, all assuming independent observations | |
| A simple question | Do male and female lizards differ in their number of dorsal scales? A t-test says no ($p \approx 0.10$). | |
| Who are their mothers? | **Think-pair-share:** "What do you notice?" The 102 lizards come from 29 mothers, and siblings are alike. | 1 |
| Hierarchical data | Naming the structure: levels, clusters, and examples from CBB research | 1 |
| Mother as a fixed effect? | It works, but spends 28 parameters on mothers we do not care about | 2 |
| The linear mixed model | Random intercepts in `lmer()`; the sex effect becomes clear | 2 |
| How alike are siblings? | Variance components and the ICC ($\rho \approx 0.44$) | 2 |
| What if $y$ is not continuous? | Binary and count outcomes; the link function | 3 |
| The GLMM | A simulated learning task with `glmer()`; odds ratios | 3, 4 |
| One thing to remember | The average curve is not the curve of the average individual | 4 |
| Before you fit a mixed model, ask... | Three questions to ask about your own data | 1, 3, 4 |

## In the full course session

After the input, students:

1. **Sketch the hierarchy** of their own dataset (5 minutes, then compare with a neighbour).
2. **Work through the [exercises](exercises.qmd)**: fit a first random-intercept model to the lizard data in the browser, then adapt the code to their own data.
3. **Compute and interpret the ICC**, and discuss: does the grouping matter for their question?
4. Take the **[self-check](self-check.qmd)** to see which ideas need another look.

## Data and materials

- Lizard data: courtesy of Prof. Geert Verbeke (KU Leuven), from the course *Concepts of Multilevel, Longitudinal and Mixed Models*.
- The learning-task data are simulated.
- Slides, code and data: [github.com/mmorenozam/demonstration-class-cbb](https://github.com/mmorenozam/demonstration-class-cbb){target="_blank"}
